title: C: Array Functions That Accept Names
description: Reading a name from the keyboard into a char array, and passing it to a function.
congratsText: Well done. You can now store a name in a char array, explain why it needs no &, and reuse the same shape for any text.
objectives: Declare a char array that can hold a name
Explain why scanf needs no & for a char array
Predict what scanf keeps when a space is typed
Apply the same name-reading shape to a new function
recap: A name is an array of letters; %s prints the whole word and %c prints one letter.
An array name is already an address, so scanf takes it without an &.
scanf("%s") stops at the first space and keeps only one word.
The same shape — void, char array, scanf with no & — works for any short text.

sections.title: A Name Is an Array of Letters

chunks.text: char name[20]; makes 20 letter-slots in a row — the same idea as an int array, only each slot holds one letter.

check.question: What does char name[20]; give you?

chunks.text: Because it is an array, name[0] is just the first letter — exactly like scores[0] was the first number.

check.question: The name holds Maria. What is inside name[0]?

chunks.text: Two different printf codes: %s prints the whole word, while %c prints one single letter.

check.question: You want the full name printed. Which code do you use?

chunks.text: For a number you wrote scanf("%d", &score);. For a name you write scanf("%s", name); — with no & at all.

check.question: Which scanf line correctly reads into char name[20]?

chunks.text: The reason is simple: an array's name is already an address. The & would ask for an address of an address, which scanf cannot use.

check.question: Why is no & needed for a char array?
options: The array name is already an address
Letters are too small to need one

chunks.text: Passing it to a function changes nothing. getName(name); hands over that same address, so the function fills the real array in main().

check.question: After getName(name); runs, does main()'s name hold what was typed?
options: Yes, the same array was filled
No, it must be returned first

quiz.question: Arrange the tokens to build a function that reads a course into a char array.

sections.title: Why Only One Word Gets In

chunks.text: scanf("%s", name); stops reading at the first space. Type Maria Clara and only Maria is stored.

check.question: You type Maria Clara into scanf("%s"). What is stored?

chunks.text: The word you lost is not deleted — it waits in line and jumps into the very next scanf without asking you again.

check.question: After typing two words, the next scanf runs. What does it do?
options: Takes the leftover word straight away
Stops and waits for fresh typing

chunks.text: None of this shows up as an error. The build stays clean, so a quiet Compile Log never proves your input arrived correctly.

check.question: Your program builds with no errors. Does that prove the full name got stored?
options: Yes, a clean build proves it

quiz.question: Type the exact word this prints.

chunks.text: One function shape covers every short text: void getCity(char text[]) reads a city exactly the way getName read a name.

check.question: Why can getCity reuse the same shape as getName?
options: Both read one word into a char array
Both send the finished word back

chunks.text: Because a char array is passed as an address, no return is ever needed — the caller's array is the one being filled.

check.question: Does getCity need a return line to hand the city back?
options: No, it filled the real array
Yes, or the city is lost

chunks.text: The space rule follows along too. getCity given Tagbilaran City keeps only the first word, just like any other %s read.

check.question: A user types Tagbilaran City into getCity. What is stored?

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: City, the last word typed in
